newsitem.title: USA: Gold prices rise sharply on dollar setback.
newsitem.headline: Gold prices rise sharply on dollar setback.

text.p: Gold prices rose sharply on Friday, boosted by the U.S. dollar's weak performance, while platinum was even stronger amid growing concern about disruptions to supplies from Russia.

Analysts said the U.S. dollar's decline, sparked by fears of central bank intervention against the currency, could produce a major turning point for gold, which sank to a four-year low earlier this year.
"The big fundamental change Friday was a huge fall in the U.S. dollar against the yen," Refco New York economist James Steel said.
Part of the reason for the fall in gold prices has been the steady rise in the U.S. dollar, making gold more expensive in many currencies, analysts said.
Gold for June delivery on COMEX in New York closed up $4.50 an ounce at $349.30.

Platinum and palladium prices rose even more sharply on tight supplies, as the flow of metal from Russia has been disrupted since December. Russia accounts for 25 percent of world platinum supplies and 60 percent of palladium supplies.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, platinum for July delivery closed $9.90 an ounce higher at $389.40, just below an earlier two month high of $389.80.

Palladium for June delivery was up six cents, the maximum permissible daily move, at a new life-of-contract high of $163.60 an ounce. In the physical market in London palladium prices were at their highest level since April 1995.

Crude oil prices extended their gains in New York after rallying sharply this week on the perception that after months of surplus, supplies are now balanced thanks to high refinery runs and fewer imports on the horizon.

"With a lot of the West African crude now heading to the Far East and runs high, supplies seem like they may remain balanced for the next 20 to 30 days," said Pat Hughes, an analyst with Chevron Corp. in California.
June crude ended nine cents higher at $20.43 a barrel. June gasoline ended 0.39 cent a gallon higher at 62.89 cents while June heating oil settled 0.14 cent a gallon higher at 54.52 cents.

The U.S. Gulf was hit with a steady stream of crude imports in March and April, particularly crude from West Africa. But Asian refineries are now absorbing imports that had been going to the United States.
Cash crude dealers said European demand is picking up as well, limiting the amount of imports of North Sea crude.
Meanwhile, the American Petroleum Institute said the U.S. refineries were running at 94.5 percent of capaity last week rising a full percentage point from the week before.
Refineries are churning out gasoline to ready gasoline inventories for the summer driving season.
On the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat prices finished higher aided by concern that cool, dry weather might cut into U.S. winter wheat production.
"A lot of the strength in the market today was in response to the drier conditions we're seeing in western Kansas," said Jason Roose, a grain analyst with U.S. Commodities.
Traders said the dry, cold weather forecast for much of the central U.S. Plains this weekend will hinder the development of the already freeze-damaged wheat crop.
Low temperatures overnight Friday in parts of northwest Kansas and southwest Nebraska fell into the low 20s Fahrenheit, according to U.S. meteorologists.
CBOT wheat for July delivery closed 4-3/4 cents a bushel higher at $4/13-3/4.
Soybean prices were also higher with buying prompted by concern about planting prospects next week amid forecasts for a cool, wet week in the U.S. Midwest.
Farmers had been planting soybeans at a record pace in some key growing states such as Illinois this year, but if forecasts prove correct, progress will inevitably slow.
CBOT soybeans for July delivery closed 5 cents a bushel higher at $8.89 a bushel.
